HEARD:

January 12, 2004

FARLEY J.
:

[
1
]        Her Majesty the Queen In
Right Of Ontario (“Applicant”) applied pursuant to (i) s. 140 of the
Courts
of Justice Act
and (ii) the inherent jurisdiction of the court to control
its own process for an order prohibiting Melvin Phil(l)ip Deutsch (“Mel”) from
commencing or continuing any civil proceeding, either directly or indirectly
through the corporate respondents or any future corporation or partnership in
which Mel may have a legal or beneficial interest, without first applying for
and obtaining leave from a judge of the Superior Court of Justice, and further
for an order prohibiting Mel from appearing as an agent before any court in
Ontario, and further for an order declaring Mel to be so ethically and
forensically incompetent so as to imperil the administration of justice if he
were to attempt to represent any party including himself.

[
2
]        At the end of the hearing, no
respondent having appeared, I granted the Applicant the relief it requested and
promised reasons.  I left the courtroom at 4:45 p.m. and checked my voicemail.
My secretary had left me a voicemail at 2:40 p.m. indicating the she had heard
from Mel who indicated that he had just received a fax from Applicant’s counsel
(which I had instructed him to send indicating that the matter would be heard
at 2:30 p.m. and that Mel should be in courtroom 803, 393 University Avenue,
Toronto at that time if he intended to contest the application), but that he
was unable to attend court.  At my request earlier in the day, Applicant’s
counsel made various calls to speak to Mel; he reported that he was successful
at 10:38 a.m., indicating that the matter was proceeding before me but that Mel
hung up on him.  He attempted to otherwise reach Mel, including calling on
Mel’s cell phone but when he was connected to the cell phone number, the call
was terminated without any response from the other end.  I note that Mel has
been aware that this application was scheduled for today - and, if necessary, for
tomorrow for some time but apparently he has chosen to ignore that in favour of
booking some unspecified medical treatment for today (12
th
January),
Wednesday (14
th
) and Thursday (15
th
) as to which he
indicated
that he would be unavailable for court between
10:30 a.m. – 2:30 p.m.  No explanation was given as to why Mel could not have
attended at 2:30 p.m. today or indeed at any time before the end of court.
Absent any valid explanation and proof of necessity for and attendance at
medical treatment, I must find that Mel is avoiding attending court.

[
3
]        Mel is an officer
and director of Fleet Rent A Car Ltd., Fleet Franchising Ltd., carrying on
business as OPEC Petroleum Co., 1341650 Ontario Ltd., carrying on business as
Deutsch, McCormick, D’Amato & Associates, U-Rent Ltd., and Fleet Car Sale
Ltd., and a partner in

Unlimited  Legal Associates.

[
4
]        The record before
me was replete with multiple convictions of Mel in the United States and Canada
for fraud and other acts of dishonesty, as to which Mel has received prison
terms of substantial time.  These offences stretch back to the beginning of the
last quarter of the 20
th
century.  As recently as September 2002,
Mel confirmed to McWatt, J. in criminal proceedings against him (for which he
was convicted by McWatt, J.) that he had been so convicted.  Included in his
offences is a conviction in New York on February 5, 1988 for conspiracy to
commit wire fraud using 113951 Canada Limited also known as Deutsch, McCormick,
D’Amato & Associates and Interworld

Paper Company to
obtain merchandise by false and fraudulent pretenses.  Mel has variously
described Deutsch, McCormick, D’Amato & Associates as a law firm and as a
firm of chartered accountants, and as a firm of business

advisors, of which he is a member, the business

being described so as to fit his perceived needs at the time.
There is no record in any of the United States jurisdictions he claims that
this firm carried on legal business, that either he or this legal firm were
registered as lawyers and admitted to the bar; similarly with respect to
Ontario and Quebec.  He uses various addresses in the U.S.A. and Canada as the
location of this non-existent firm.

[
5
]        On February
13, 1998, Mel was ordered deported from the U.S.A.   In the immigration
proceedings he was found to have lied by Judge Reese as to his true identity.
Indeed Judge Reese found that he had expropriated the identity of an American
cousin and then also attempted to show without success that another cousin had
impersonated Mel and done the illegal acts.

[
6
]        McWatt, J.
sentenced Mel to 4 years imprisonment on January 17, 2003 for fraud over $5,000
and possession of stolen property over $5,000; Mel has appealed that
conviction.

[
7
]        Mel’s dishonesty
goes beyond the criminal sphere; notwithstanding that he has never been
qualified as a lawyer, he has consistently held himself out as a lawyer and
purporting thereby to represent not only himself but others.  In Ontario, this
reached as far back as Feb. 1984 when he filed a writ of summons in the Supreme
Court of Ontario in which he falsely identified himself as a solicitor for the
plaintiff.  In the spring of 1984 as well he applied to practice law in Ontario
and that as “the Dean of The John George Diefenbaker Memoral (
sic
)
University School of Law” he met the LSUC requirements.  In 1985, MacKinnon
A.C.J.O. noted in
Canadian Imperial Bank of Commerce v. Dencare Building
Cleaning Co.
,
[1985]

O.J. No. 45 (C.A.)
that: “The appellant
[Mel] attempted to deliberately mislead the Court which is a serious

act and does not compel sympathy for his position.”

[
8
]        Mel abused
judicial offices when in April 1982 he submitted a false application for an
appointment as a Commissioner for Taking Oaths.  In the January 1990 decision
of
United States v. Bradley
, the Court of Appeals for the U.S. 7
th

Circuit refused standing to Mel after investigating his claimed legal
credentials; Esterbrook, J. for the Court concluded: “Deutsch is a con-man, a
fraud, a

phony, a humbug, a mountebank - in short,
an imposter.”  In February 1990, that

court revisited the claimed
legal credentials of

Mel
and his firm Deutsch, McCormick, D’Amato & Associates and Esterbrook, J.
for the Court concluded:   “All of this suggests that Deutsch and his cohorts
are going into business in a big way.  P.T. Barnhem would have been proud.”  In

Melvin P. Deutsch v. United States

67 F. 3d 1080
, Mel was found to have
engaged in filing a frivolous claim.  In 1995 Judge Korman of the U.S. District
Court for the Eastern District of New York in an unreported decision stated:
“The time has come to place some restraints on the barrage of frivolous
complaints.  Accordingly the Clerk is directed not to accept any papers,
proceedings, motions or new cases of any kind presented by Mr. Melvin Deutsch
without the

permission
of a United States Magistrate Judge.” Mel, however, when confronted with those
types of decisions bombards

the judicial officials and counsel on the other side with
threatened litigation (including sending unfiled proceedings to them) and
corresponding with them (one sided) indicating that they are biased,

dishonest
, incompetent, or
other adjectives of a derogatory nature, all without any scintilla of
foundation.

[
9
]        In 1999, the City
of Toronto prosecuted Fleet Rent A Car Ltd. for numerous parking violations.
Mel, purportedly of the firm Deutsch, McCormick, D’Amato & Associates,
acted as agent for the defendant and some others.   Between August and December
1999, Mel served at least 647 motions to stay, dismiss or quash charges for
delay, failure to disclose and other alleged
Charter
breaches.  This
included 156 motions for French trials, notwithstanding that Mel has
consistently been found to be incapable of reasonably
communicating
in oral and
written French.  Indeed he has submitted in applying to act
pro bono
in
giving legal advice that his languages were English and Jewish (Yiddish).
Mel’s second appointment as a Commissioner for Taking Oaths (which slipped by
the granting authority) was used by Mel contrary to its terms (it being for use
in regard to the
accounting
practice of Deutsch, McCormick, D’Amato
& Associates) and not as was done by him in
relation to

legal
litigation.  Following the revocation of his
appointment as a Commissioner, he commissioned at least one further affidavit
two months later for use in a case:
Fleet Rent A Car Ltd. v. Luigi Rachiele
.

[
10
]      As recently as
January 2002, Mel purported that he and his colleagues McCormick and D’Amato
were attorneys admitted to practice in New York.  Justice Thomson caught him
out in this fabrication.  In October 2002, I similarly caught him out in the
same lie in finding that he could not represent a corporate party of which he
was an officer.  I also found him to be incompetent in being able to represent
anyone, in part because of his unfamiliarity with basic legal principles.

[
11
]      On August 6,
2002 Mel attempted to have an unissued application heard with a number of
criminal matters scheduled before Grossi, J.   Applicant’s counsel attended on
short notice and had the application struck out.

[
12
]      On September
13, 2002 Mel attempted to requisition Crown defendants in default on the
strength of an affidavit falsely claiming that all defendants had been served.

[
13
]      In August 2002,
Mel of Deutsch, McCormick, D’Amato & Associates, now purporting to be of
Chicago served the Crown with a Statement of Claim in
Melvin P. Deutsch v.
Her Majesty The Queen et al.
, Court File No. 02-CV-233506-CM1 in which he
claims damages of $100 billion plus punitive damages

making

wide-ranging bald
allegations amongst numerous individuals, including Mel Lastman, Julian
Fantino, Michael Harris, Ernie Eves, David Young, and a total of 275 John
Does.

[
14
]      Mel has been
variously found in the US courts to have been engaging in frivolous and
vexatious litigation; it appears that old habits die hard and he is continuing
that practice in Ontario.

[
15
]      Section 140 of
the
Courts of Justice Act
provides
inter alia
:

s.140 (1)
Vexatious
proceedings —
Where a judge of the Superior Court of Justice is satisfied,
on application, that a person has persistently and without reasonable grounds,

(1)

instituted vexatious proceedings
in any court; or

(2)

conducted a proceeding in any
court in a vexatious manner, the judge may order that,

(3)

no further proceedings be
instituted by the person in any court; or

(4)

a proceeding previously instituted
by the person in any court not be continued,

except by leave of a judge of the
Superior Court of Justice.

s.140 (3)
Application for
leave to proceed —
Where a person against whom an order under subsection
(1) has been made seeks leave to institute or continue a proceeding, the person
shall do so by way of an application in the Superior Court of Justice.

s.140 (5)
Abuse of process
—
Nothing in this section limits the authority of a court to stay or dismiss
a proceeding as an abuse of process or on any other ground.

[
16
]      In
Foy v. Foy

(No.
2)

(1979),
1979 CanLII 1631 (ON CA)
,
26 O.R. (2d) 220 (C.A.)
at pp. 225-6
, Howland C.J.O. stated:

Vexatious proceedings legislation does not take away an
individual’s right to redress.  Rather it provides that if an order is made
against him under the legislation, he cannot seek redress until he has
satisfied the proper authority that the proposed legal proceedings are not an
abuse of process of the Court and there is prima facie ground for them.

The word “vexatious” has not been clearly defined.
Under the Act the legal proceedings must be vexatious and must also have been
instituted without reasonable ground.  In many of the reported decisions the
legal proceedings were held to be vexatious because they were instituted
without any reasonable ground.  As a result the proceedings were found to
constitute an abuse of process of the Court.  An example of such proceedings is
the bringing of one or more actions to determine an issue which has already
been determined by a Court of competent jurisdiction...

[
17
]      Blair, J.A. in the same case
at p. 237 observed:

I agree with Chief Justice Howland’s interpretation of
the word “vexatious” based on his careful examination of the authorities.  It
is plain that the word “vexatious” as used in this Act is broadly synonymous
with the concept of abuse of process developed by the Courts in the exercise of
their inherent right to control proceedings.  The jurisdiction to strike out or
stay proceedings as an abuse of process is not, as the authorities make clear,
limited to actions or other originating proceedings.  It applies to appeals and
interlocutory proceedings of all kinds.

The concept of abuse of process protects the public
interest in the integrity and fairness of the judicial system.  It does so by
preventing the employment of judicial proceedings for purposes which the law
regards as improper.  These improper purposes include harassment and oppression
of other parties by multifarious proceedings which are brought by purposes
other than the assertion or defence of a litigant’s legitimate rights.  Such
abuse of process interferes with the business of the Courts and tarnishes their
image in the administration of justice.

[
18
]      In

Mascan Corp. v. French

(1988),
1988 CanLII 4731 (ON CA)
,
64 O.R. (2d) 1 (C.A.)
, the Court of
Appeal confirmed that the 1984 change to s. 140 of the
Courts of Justice Act

was intended so that court would have authority to consider
any

proceeding
.

[
19
]      Within the last few years,
there have been decisions which confirm that s. 140 is not restricted to
plaintiffs but rather would include defendants and anyone else responding to a
proceeding: see
National Bank of Canada v. Fitzmaier
,
[2002] O.J. No.
567 (Sup. Ct.)
at para. 34
;
Beattie v. Ladouceur
(2001),
2001 CanLII 28166 (ON SC)
,
23 R.F.L. (5
th
)
33 (Ont. Sup. Ct.)
at p. 63
.

[
20
]      In
Re Lang Michener et al.
v. Fabian et al.

(1987),
1987 CanLII 172 (ON HCJ)
,
59 O.R. (2d) 353 (H.C.J.)
at pp. 358-9
, Henry J.
reviewed
Foy
,
supra
,
Re Kitchener-Waterloo Record Ltd. and
Weber

(1986),
1986 CanLII 2715 (ON HCJ)
,
53 O.R. (2d) 687 (Ont. S.C.)
and
Re Law Society of Upper
Canada and Zikov
(1984),
47 C.P.C. 42 (Ont. S.C.)
and summarized the
characteristics of vexatious proceedings as follows:

From these decisions the following principles may be
extracted:

(a)

the bringing of one or more
actions to determine an issue which has already been determined by a court of
competent jurisdiction constitutes a vexatious proceeding;

(b)

where it is obvious that an action
cannot succeed, or if the action would lead to no possible good, or if no
reasonable person can reasonably expect to obtain relief, the action is
vexatious;

(c)

vexatious actions include those
brought for an improper purpose, including the harassment and oppression of
other parties by multifarious proceedings brought for purposes other than the
assertion of legitimate rights;

(d)

it is a general characteristic of
vexatious proceedings that grounds and issues raised tend to be rolled forward
into subsequent actions and repeated and supplemented, often with actions
brought against the lawyers who have acted for or against the litigant in
earlier proceedings;

(e)

in determining whether proceedings
are vexatious, the court must look at the whole history of the matter and not
just whether there was originally a good cause of action;

(f)

the failure of the person
instituting the proceedings to pay the costs of unsuccessful proceedings is one
factor to be considered in determining whether proceedings are vexatious;

(g)

the respondent’s conduct in
persistently taking unsuccessful appeals from judicial decisions can be
considered vexatious conduct of legal proceedings.

[
21
]      The categories of vexatious
proceedings are never closed and must be determined by an objective standard:
see
Mascan
,
supra
, at p. 7;
Law Society of Upper Canada v.
Chavali

(1998),
21 C.P.C. (4
th
) 20 (Ont. Gen. Div.)
at pp. 25-6
,
affirmed
(1998),
37 C.P.C. (4
th
) 221 (C.A.)
;
Children’s Aid
Society of Ottawa-Carlton v. M.B.
,
[1997] O.J. No. 1964 (Gen. Div.)
at
para. 22
.

[
22
]      From the
foregoing findings there is overwhelming evidence that Mel has persistently and
habitually abused the process of the courts of Ontario.

[
23
]      Section 50 of the
Law
Society Act
prohibits non-lawyers from practicing law “except where
otherwise provided by law”.  Mel does not fit within this

exception.  An unauthorized
agent who represents another person before a court or a tribunal is engaged in
the practice of law contrary to the
Law Society Act
(and s. 1 of the
Solicitors
Act
).  The following activities engaged in by Mel would be unauthorized –
corresponding with opposing counsel, preparing and arguing motions, conducting
examinations for discovery or cross-examinations, attending case conferences or
other interlocutory proceedings, all for the purported benefit of a third
party.  Mel has consistently been found not suitable to represent a corporation
pursuant to R. 15.01.  In the absence of a statutory provision, it lies within
a court’s discretion whether to permit a person who is not a lawyer to
represent a litigant; the B.C. Court of Appeal recently confirmed that in such
cases, the court confers a “privilege” of an audience on the agent who is not a
lawyer:

see
R.
v. Dick

(2002),
2002 BCCA 27 (CanLII)
,
163 B.C.A.C. 62 (C.A.)
at p. 64
.

[
24
]      There are strong public policy reasons for the general
rule excluding agents, as each court has the responsibility that persons
appearing before it are properly represented and to maintain the rule of law
and the integrity of the court generally.  Some statues, e.g. the
Provincial
Offences Act
, expressly provide for representation by an agent but that
legislation goes on to provide that a court may exclude an agent who does not
understand and comply with the duties and responsibilities of an agent.  See
also s. 26 of the
Courts of Justice Act
.  The purpose of these
provisions is to protect the parties and the court from incompetent or
unscrupulous agents.  The power to disqualify agents extends to those whose
forensic skills are so wanting as to render their participation in a proceeding
a real hindrance

both for the party for whom they act and
to the court.  The power to disqualify agents also extends to those who are
ethically incompetent in that they cannot be relied upon to conduct their
principal’s representation in an honest and ethical manner.  The court must be
able to rely upon the integrity, honesty, and forthrightness of agents who
appear before it.
See
R. v. Romanowicz
(1999),
1999 CanLII 1315 (ON CA)
,
45 O.R. (3d) 506 (C.A.)

at pp. 523-4
;
Codina v. Law Society of Upper Canada

(1996),
93 O.A.C.
214 (Div. Ct.)
;
Kopyto v. Ontario (Attorney General)
(1997);
Roberts
v. Senior

(2003),
2003 CanLII 64818 (ON CJ)
,
35 R.F.L. (5
th
) 440
at p. 447
.

[
25
]
Romanowicz
,

supra
, at pp. 523-4 confirms that the court has inherent authority to
disqualify agents by virtue of the court’s power to control its own process.
The Court of Appeal held at pp. 525, 527-8 as follows:

A power to deny audience to an agent whose
participation in proceedings would either damage the fairness of those
proceedings, impair the ability of the tribunal to perform its function or
otherwise undermine the integrity of the process is entirely consistent with
the exercise of the power recognized in the authorities referred to

above.  Surely, representation by an agent
who has been shown to be incompetent or disreputable can imperil the accused’s
right to a fair trial and can undermine the integrity of the proceedings just
as much as if an accused who was incapable of representing himself were
required to proceed without counsel.

It is impossible to catalogue
all of the circumstances in which representation by a particular agent would
imperil the administration of justice and properly call for an order
disqualifying that agent.  Obviously, representation by agents lacking the
ability to competently represent an accused endangers all aspects of the proper
administration of justice, particularly the accused’s right to a fair trial.
Other examples where the administration of justice would suffer irreparable
harm if an agent were allowed to appear are found in the material filed on this
appeal.  They include representation by an agent facing criminal charges involving
interference with the administration of justice and representation by an agent
whose background demonstrates pervasive dishonesty or a blatant disrespect for
the law.  Representation by persons who have convictions for crimes of
dishonesty or who have otherwise demonstrated a lack of good character can only
bring the administration of justice into disrepute in the eyes of reasonable
members of the public.  This is so even if those agents have the requisite
forensic ability.  We emphasize, however, that we do not suggest that a
criminal record or some discreditable conduct automatically disqualifies
someone from representing an accused.  We are referring to situations in which
the agent’s criminal record or other discreditable acts are such as to permit
the conclusion that the agent cannot be relied on to conduct a trial ethically
and honourably.

[
26
]      The foregoing
demonstrates (and the record is replete)
with
instances that
Mel is forensically and ethically
incompetent in that he has been convicted of crimes of dishonesty, he has made
various false statements and misrepresentations to the court, he has abused his
Commissioner and Notary Public appointments, he does not understand basic legal
principles, and he does not understand (or care to adhere to) the duties and

obligations of an agent or
representative.  If Mel believes what he has misrepresented to the court, then
I must conclude he
is delusional;

if he does not so believe then the only alternative is that
he is being deceitful to the court and disrespectful of the system of justice.

[
27
]      Without
any control (which is more than reasonably necessary in Mel’s case), Mel will
continue to run rampant through the judicial system in Ontario, without any
apparent thought or concern for the administration of justice and the integrity
of the justice system.  Furthermore, he will, it appears, needlessly clog up
the courts, waste scarce judicial resources and preclude others in other cases
from obtaining timely access to the courts.

[
28
]      Accordingly the
order to which I affixed my fiat is more than amply justified.  In my view the
award of $10,000 costs against Mel is quite reasonable in the circumstances
given the work involved as required by this application.

J.
M. Farley

Released:

January 12, 2004
